title: Pagination Optimization
description: Implement keyset and cursor-based pagination to replace slow OFFSET queries

data.text: OFFSET pagination becomes slow on large tables because the database must scan and discard rows. Keyset pagination uses a WHERE clause on the last-seen values for stable, fast paging.

data.title: Comparison
items: OFFSET: simple but degrades with deep pages
Keyset: stable timing regardless of page depth
Cursor: opaque token for stateless APIs
Seek method: same as keyset with an index

data.title: Keyset pagination
data.content: Use a composite unique key for deterministic paging.
data.code:
-- Slow OFFSET
SELECT * FROM products
ORDER BY created_at DESC, product_id DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000;

-- Fast keyset
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE (created_at, product_id) < ('2024-01-01', 5678)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, product_id DESC
LIMIT 20;

data.title: Warning
data.text: Keyset pagination requires a unique, immutable sort column. Avoid mutable columns like popularity scores as sort keys.

items.question: When is OFFSET acceptable?
items.answer: For shallow pages under 1000 rows on small tables. Do not use OFFSET for deep paging on large tables.

items.question: What if I need total count?
items.answer: Keyset pagination does not need total count. If needed, cache it or estimate with approximate counts.

items.question: How do I handle ties in sort keys?
items.answer: Use a unique tiebreaker column like an auto-incrementing ID as the second sort key.

data.title: Summary
points: Use keyset pagination with unique sort keys
Include a tiebreaker for duplicate sort values
data.takeaway: Keyset pagination provides consistent performance and stable results for large result sets.
